title: B cells and antibodies
covers: The humoral response: how B cells are activated with and without T-cell help, what happens in the germinal center, and what each antibody class does.

items.p: A T cell needs two signals: its receptor on peptide–MHC, then costimulation. It then proliferates, makes cytokines and becomes an effector cell.

ul: CD28 (T cell) binds B7 (APC): the costimulatory signal
CD40L (activated CD4 T cell) binds CD40 on B cells, macrophages and dendritic cells
Signal 1 without proper costimulation can lead to anergy

items.p: Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells with perforin (holes) and enzymes that trigger apoptosis.
B cells are made and mature in the bone marrow. Naive B cells carry IgM and IgD (by alternative splicing) and meet antigen in peripheral lymphoid tissue.

ul: Follicular B cells: the majority; T-dependent responses to proteins; long-lived plasma cells
Marginal zone and B-1 cells: T-independent responses to lipids, polysaccharides, nucleic acids
Memory B cells: membrane-bound antibody, long life

summary.h: Two ways to activate a B cell

items.p: Signal 1 always comes from the B-cell receptor. Signal 2 differs.

ul: T-independent: repetitive non-protein antigens cross-link receptors (TI-2) or add a TLR signal (TI-1). Little or no memory.
T-dependent: protein antigens. The B cell presents peptide to a Tfh cell and receives CD40L and cytokines.

items.p: Complement helps: CD21 (CR2) binds complement on the microbe and brings CD19 to the receptor, boosting the signal. The coreceptor is CD19, CD21 and CD81.

items.note: The take-home slide lists the coreceptor as "CD19/CD20/CD81" and says T-dependent activation is by "type 2 helper T cells". The detailed slides say CD19/CD21/CD81 and Tfh cells; these match standard texts.

items.p: Fewer than 1 in 10,000 naive T cells recognize a given antigen, so T and B cells must be steered together.

ul: Lymph flow: afferent vessel, subcapsular sinus, cortex, medulla, efferent vessel
Naive T cells sit in T-cell areas; naive B cells in primary follicles
Follicular dendritic cells are not hematopoietic and not phagocytic; they hold antigen on complement receptors for B cells
Activated B and T cells move to the follicle border and meet: linked recognition

items.p: Tfh signals: CD40L gives survival (NFκB, anti-apoptotic proteins). IL-21 gives proliferation and plasma-cell differentiation (STAT3).
First phase: B cells proliferate in the primary focus. Some become plasmablasts: still dividing, secreting mainly IgM, dead within days.

Second phase: other B cells enter the follicle with Tfh cells and build a germinal center. The follicle is now a secondary follicle, with a mantle zone of resting B cells around a light and a dark zone. It disappears 3–4 weeks after exposure.
The enzyme AID mutates the V region (somatic hypermutation), about 1 per 1000 base pairs per division.

ul: Higher affinity: survival, with help from Tfh cells and CD40
Good binders re-enter the dark zone and divide again
Survivors become plasma cells or memory cells

items.p: The V region stays; the constant region changes. It is an irreversible DNA recombination between switch regions (every C gene has one except δ), directed by Tfh cytokines.
Enzymes in order: AID, UNG, APE1. They nick both strands, the DNA between two switch regions is cut out, and the ends are joined.

table: First antibody; pentamer, 10 sites; high avidity; strong complement activator; stays in blood
Main antibody in blood and tissue fluid (about 80%); 3-week life; opsonizes; fixes complement; crosses the placenta; 4 subclasses
Main antibody in secretions and breast milk; neutralizes; monomer or dimer; 2 subclasses
Very low level; bound to mast cells; allergy and parasites
On naive B cells with IgM; hardly secreted

items.p: Antibodies work by neutralization, opsonization and complement activation. In ADCC, NK cells bind the Fc of antibody on a target and kill it; this matters against parasites.

items.note: The slide says IgG crosses the placenta "because of its size". Standard texts attribute transfer to a specific Fc receptor in the placenta.

cards.q: CD28 binds what, and why does it matter?
cards.a: B7 (B7-1, B7-2) on APCs; it is the costimulatory second signal for T-cell activation.

cards.q: CD40L: which cell carries it and what does it bind?
cards.a: Activated CD4 T cells; binds CD40 on B cells, macrophages and dendritic cells.

cards.q: Th1, Th2, Th17: signature cytokines
cards.a: Th1: IFN-γ. Th2: IL-4, IL-5, IL-13. Th17: IL-17, IL-22.

cards.q: Which T helper subset helps B cells in germinal centers, and with which cytokine?
cards.a: T follicular helper (Tfh) cells; IL-21

cards.q: Which immunoglobulins are on a naive B cell?
cards.a: IgM and IgD (co-expressed by alternative splicing)

cards.q: Which B cells make T-independent responses?
cards.a: Marginal zone B cells and B-1 cells (follicular B cells make T-dependent responses)

cards.q: Typical T-independent antigens, and the catch
cards.a: Repetitive non-protein polymers (polysaccharides, glycolipids, nucleic acids); little or no memory

cards.q: TI-1 versus TI-2
cards.a: TI-1: BCR plus another receptor such as a TLR. TI-2: strong cross-linking of BCRs by repetitive polysaccharide.

cards.q: The B-cell coreceptor complex
cards.a: CD19, CD21 (CR2) and CD81; CD21 binds complement on the microbe

cards.q: Follicular dendritic cells: three facts
cards.a: Non-hematopoietic, non-phagocytic, hold antigen on complement receptors for B cells

cards.q: Linked recognition
cards.a: T and B cells activated by the same antigen meet at the follicle–T-zone border

cards.q: What do CD40L and IL-21 from Tfh cells do to the B cell?
cards.a: CD40L: survival (NFκB, anti-apoptotic). IL-21: proliferation and plasma-cell differentiation (STAT3).

cards.q: Plasmablast versus plasma cell
cards.a: Plasmablast: still dividing, mainly IgM, short-lived, in the primary focus. Plasma cell: long-lived, goes to the bone marrow.

cards.q: What is a secondary lymphoid follicle?
cards.a: A follicle containing a germinal center (mantle zone around light and dark zones)

cards.q: Enzyme of somatic hypermutation, and the region it changes
cards.a: AID (activation-induced cytidine deaminase); the V region, not the C region

cards.q: What is class switching, molecularly?
cards.a: Irreversible non-homologous recombination between switch regions; same V region, new constant region

cards.q: Enzymes of class-switch recombination, in order
cards.a: AID, UNG, APE1

cards.q: Which heavy-chain gene has no switch region?
cards.a: δ (IgD is made by alternative splicing, not switching)

cards.q: IgM: structure and strengths
cards.a: Pentamer with 10 binding sites; high avidity; best complement activator; first antibody made

cards.q: IgG: four key properties
cards.a: Main antibody of blood and extracellular fluid, about 3-week life, opsonin and complement activator, crosses the placenta

cards.q: IgA: where and how it works
cards.a: Secretions and breast milk; mainly neutralization; monomer or dimer

cards.q: IgE
cards.a: Very low level; bound to mast cells (and basophils); allergic reactions and parasite defense

cards.q: Three ways antibodies protect
cards.a: Neutralization, opsonization, complement activation

cards.q: ADCC
cards.a: NK cells recognize the Fc of antibody bound to a target and kill it; important against parasites

cards.q: Fate of B cells leaving the germinal center
cards.a: Plasma cells (bone marrow, medullary cords, splenic red pulp) or memory B cells

questions.stem: After receiving signals 1 and 2, what does a T cell do next, and where does signal 2 originate according to the lecture?

options.A: Proliferation, antibody secretion and differentiation into plasma cells; from molecules produced during the innate response
options.B: Proliferation, cytokine production and effector differentiation; from molecules produced during the innate response
options.C: Anergy followed by apoptosis; from molecules produced during the adaptive response
options.D: Somatic hypermutation and class switching; from cytokines released by follicular dendritic cells
options.E: Proliferation, cytokine production and differentiation into its effector state; from peptide bound in the MHC groove

questions.explanation: Through secondary signals the T cell proliferates, produces cytokines and differentiates into its effector state. Signal 2 results from molecules produced during the innate immune response (costimulators, cytokines, complement products). A: Antibody secretion and plasma cells describe B cells. C: Anergy results from negative costimulatory signaling. D: These are B-cell processes. E: Peptide–MHC is signal 1.

questions.stem: Which pairing of costimulatory molecule, expressing cell and ligand is correct?

options.A: CD28 on T cells binds B7 on APCs; CD40L on activated CD4+ T cells binds CD40 on B cells
options.B: CD28 on APCs binds B7-1 and B7-2 on T cells; CD40L on B cells binds CD40 on activated CD4+ T cells
options.C: CD40L on T cells binds B7-1 and B7-2 on APCs; CD28 on activated CD4+ T cells binds CD40 on B cells
options.D: CD28 on T cells binds CD40 on APCs; CD40L on activated CD8+ T cells binds B7 on B cells
options.E: CD21 on T cells binds B7-1 on APCs; CD40L on NK cells binds CD40 on dendritic cells

questions.explanation: CD28 (T cells) binds B7-1/B7-2 on APCs: costimulatory signal for T-cell activation. CD40L (activated CD4+ T cells) binds CD40 on B cells, macrophages and DCs: activates APCs and promotes B-cell help. B: Both pairs are reversed. C: The ligands are swapped. D: CD28 binds B7, and CD40L is on activated CD4+ T cells. E: CD21 is part of the B-cell coreceptor.

questions.stem: Besides activation, what can some costimulatory signals produce?

options.A: Negative T-cell signaling with class switching to IgE
options.B: Positive selection of high-affinity T-cell clones in germinal centers
options.C: Irreversible rearrangement of the T-cell receptor genes
options.D: Release of perforin from the antigen-presenting cell
options.E: Negative signaling with cellular anergy

questions.explanation: Some costimulatory signals lead to negative T-cell signaling, resulting in cellular anergy; these pathways may also be involved in generating regulatory cells. A: Class switching is a B-cell event. B: Selection in germinal centers concerns B cells. C: Rearrangement occurs during development. D: Perforin is released by cytotoxic cells.

questions.stem: Which CD4 T-cell subset is matched with its cytokines and target microbes as in the lecture figure?

options.A: Th17: IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13; helminth parasites
options.B: Th2: IFN-γ; microbes persisting in macrophage vesicles
options.C: Th1: IL-21; isotype switching against extracellular bacteria
options.D: Th17: IL-17 and IL-22; extracellular bacteria and fungi
options.E: Tfh: IL-17 and IL-22; fungi at epithelial surfaces

questions.explanation: Th1: IFN-γ, macrophage activation, microbes persisting in macrophage vesicles. Th2: IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, eosinophils/mast cells/basophils, helminths. Th17: IL-17, IL-22, neutrophils, extracellular bacteria and fungi. Tfh: IL-21, B-cell help. Treg: inhibition. A: That profile belongs to Th2. B: That profile belongs to Th1. C: IL-21 and B-cell help belong to Tfh. E: That profile belongs to Th17.

questions.stem: Which T-cell subset helps B cells in germinal centers to produce antibody, and which subset in the same figure targets helminth parasites?

options.A: T follicular helper cells; Th17 cells
options.B: Th1 cells; Th2 cells
options.C: T follicular helper cells; Th2 cells
options.D: Regulatory T cells; Th1 cells
options.E: Th2 cells; T follicular helper cells

questions.explanation: T follicular helper (Tfh) cells help B cells in germinal centers; Th2 cells act through eosinophils, mast cells and basophils against helminth parasites. A: Th17 targets extracellular bacteria and fungi. B: Th1 activates macrophages. D: Regulatory T cells inhibit responses. E: Reversed.

questions.stem: In the T-cell mediated cytotoxic response, what is the correct sequence?

options.A: Cytotoxic T cell binds the infected cell; an enzyme makes holes in its membrane; perforin enters and promotes apoptosis
options.B: Helper T cell binds the infected cell; perforin makes holes in its membrane; complement enters and causes lysis
options.C: Cytotoxic T cell binds free antigen; antibody makes holes in the microbe; an enzyme enters and promotes necrosis
options.D: Cytotoxic T cell binds the infected cell; perforin makes holes in its membrane; an enzyme enters and promotes apoptosis
options.E: Cytotoxic T cell engulfs the infected cell; lysosomal enzymes digest it in a phagolysosome

questions.explanation: The cytotoxic T cell binds the infected cell (self–nonself complex), perforin makes holes in the infected cell's membrane, an enzyme that promotes apoptosis enters, and the infected cell is destroyed. A: Perforin forms the holes and the enzyme enters. B: The killer is the cytotoxic T cell, and complement is not involved. C: The T cell binds a self–nonself complex on an infected cell. E: Killing is by perforin and enzymes, not phagocytosis.

questions.stem: Which statement about B-cell development and activation is correct?

options.A: B cells are produced in the bone marrow and mature in the thymus; antigen binds IgM and IgD on mature naive B cells
options.B: B cells are produced and mature in the bone marrow; antigen binds IgG and IgA on mature naive B cells
options.C: B cells are produced in lymph nodes and mature in the spleen; antigen binds IgM on plasma cells
options.D: B cells are produced and mature in the bone marrow; antigen binds peptide–MHC II on naive B cells
options.E: B cells are produced and mature in the bone marrow; antigen binds IgM and IgD on mature naive B cells

questions.explanation: B cells are produced and mature in the bone marrow, then migrate to peripheral lymphoid tissues. Antigens bind IgM and IgD on mature naive B cells, leading to activation, proliferation and differentiation into antibody-secreting plasma cells. A: Thymic maturation applies to T cells. B: Naive B cells carry IgM and IgD. C: Production and maturation are in the bone marrow. D: B cells bind antigen through surface immunoglobulin.

questions.stem: How are memory B cells described, and what kinds of antigen do B cells recognize?

options.A: Secreted antibodies and a short lifespan; extracellular soluble antigens and cell surface antigens
options.B: Membrane-bound antibodies and a long lifespan; soluble antigens and cell surface antigens
options.C: Membrane-bound antibodies and a long lifespan; processed peptides on MHC molecules
options.D: No immunoglobulin and a long lifespan; intracellular antigens in the cytosol
options.E: Membrane-bound antibodies and a lifespan of days; soluble antigens exclusively

questions.explanation: Memory B cells have membrane-bound antibodies and a long lifespan. B cells recognize extracellular soluble antigens and cell surface antigens. A: Memory cells carry membrane-bound antibody and are long-lived. C: That is T-cell recognition. D: Memory B cells have membrane Ig, and B cells see extracellular or surface antigen. E: They are long-lived and also recognize cell surface antigens.

questions.stem: On the B-cell receptor, what are Fab and Fc, and how does a naive B cell express IgM and IgD together?

options.A: Fab: antigen-binding fragment; Fc: constant fragment; by alternative splicing
options.B: Fab: constant fragment; Fc: antigen-binding fragment; by alternative splicing
options.C: Fab: antigen-binding fragment; Fc: constant fragment; by class-switch recombination
options.D: Fab: light chain; Fc: heavy chain; by somatic hypermutation
options.E: Fab: antigen-binding fragment; Fc: complement fragment; by V(D)J recombination of a second allele

questions.explanation: Fab = fragment antigen binding; Fc = constant fragment. IgM and IgD are co-expressed through alternative splicing of the heavy-chain transcript (μ and δ constant genes). B: The fragments are swapped. C: IgD co-expression does not involve switch recombination. D: Fab contains parts of both chains, and hypermutation changes V regions. E: Fc is the constant fragment.

questions.stem: Which B-cell subset is matched with its response?

options.A: Follicular B cells: T-independent responses to polysaccharides; marginal zone and B-1 cells: T-dependent responses to proteins
options.B: Follicular B cells: T-dependent responses to lipids; B-1 cells: long-lived plasma cells against proteins
options.C: Follicular B cells: T-dependent responses to proteins; marginal zone and B-1 cells: T-independent responses
options.D: Marginal zone B cells: germinal center responses to proteins; follicular B cells: mucosal responses to nucleic acids
options.E: B-1 cells: the majority of B cells in follicles; follicular B cells: a minority in mucosal sites

questions.explanation: Follicular B cells (the majority) make the bulk of T-dependent responses to protein antigens and give rise to long-lived plasma cells. T-independent responses to multivalent antigens (lipids, polysaccharides, nucleic acids) come mainly from marginal zone B cells and B-1 cells in mucosal sites. A: Reversed. B: Follicular cells answer protein antigens and give long-lived plasma cells. D: Reversed. E: Follicular B cells are the majority.

questions.stem: B-cell activation needs a signal from the BCR plus a second signal. Which statement about signal 2 is correct?

options.A: It comes from microbial antigens for protein antigens, or from Tfh cells in T-independent activation
options.B: It comes from follicular dendritic cells for protein antigens, or from NK cells otherwise
options.C: It comes from CD28 on the B cell binding B7 on the T cell
options.D: It comes from Tfh cells for protein antigens, or from microbial antigens in T-independent activation
options.E: It comes from complement for protein antigens and is absent in T-independent activation

questions.explanation: Signal 1 is from the BCR. Signal 2 is from Tfh cells (T-dependent, protein antigens) or from microbial antigens (T-independent; not applicable for protein antigens). A: Reversed; microbial signal 2 is not applicable to protein antigens. B: Not the sources given. C: CD28 is on T cells. E: T-independent activation has a microbial second signal.

questions.stem: A polysaccharide capsule with highly repetitive units activates B cells directly. Which statement fits this type of activation?

options.A: The antigen cross-links B-cell receptors, and abundant memory cells are generated
options.B: The antigen cross-links B-cell receptors, and little or no memory is generated
options.C: The antigen is presented on MHC II to Tfh cells, and little or no memory is generated
options.D: The antigen needs linked recognition at the follicle border, and class switching is extensive
options.E: The antigen is a protein that binds a single receptor, and germinal centers form

questions.explanation: T-independent activation: non-protein polymeric antigens with highly repetitive units (bacterial polysaccharides, glycolipids, nucleic acids) cross-link BCRs or are received with a TLR; this generates no or little memory. A: T-independent activation gives little or no memory. C: That would be T-dependent. D: That describes T-dependent responses. E: T-independent antigens are non-protein, polymeric and repetitive.

questions.stem: How do TI-1 and TI-2 activation differ?

options.A: TI-1: BCR plus other receptors such as TLR; TI-2: strong BCR cross-linking by repetitive polysaccharides
options.B: TI-1: strong cross-linking of the BCR by repetitive polysaccharides; TI-2: simultaneous activation of the BCR and TLR
options.C: TI-1: activation by Tfh cells through CD40; TI-2: activation by complement through CD21
options.D: TI-1: activation of follicular B cells; TI-2: activation of plasma cells
options.E: TI-1: protein antigens; TI-2: lipid antigens presented on MHC II

questions.explanation: TI-1: simultaneous activation of BCR and other receptors on B cells (such as TLR). TI-2: strong cross-linking of BCR by repetitive polysaccharides. B: Reversed. C: Tfh help defines T-dependent activation. D: Not the distinction given. E: T-independent antigens are non-protein.

questions.stem: Why must the migration of activated T and B cells in secondary lymphoid organs be precisely regulated?

options.A: More than 1/100 naive T cells recognize a given antigen, so encounters must be limited
options.B: Naive B cells cannot bind antigen until a T cell has processed it
options.C: T cells and B cells recognize different antigens in linked recognition
options.D: Fewer than 1/10,000 B cells express immunoglobulin, so T cells must select them
options.E: Fewer than 1/10,000 naive T cells recognize a given antigen

questions.explanation: The frequency of naive T cells recognizing a particular antigen is extremely low (<1/10,000), so linked recognition requires regulated migration of activated T and B cells into specific locations. A: The frequency is extremely low. B: B cells bind native antigen. C: Linked recognition involves the same antigen. D: The figure refers to naive T cells specific for an antigen.

questions.stem: Trace lymph through a lymph node and state why the node acts as a "settling tank".

options.A: Afferent lymphatics, medulla, cortex, subcapsular sinus, efferent vessel; there are fewer efferent vessels
options.B: Efferent lymphatics, subcapsular sinus, cortex, medulla, afferent vessel; there are fewer afferent vessels
options.C: Afferent lymphatics, subcapsular sinus, cortex, medulla, efferent vessel; there are fewer efferent vessels
options.D: Afferent lymphatics, cortex, subcapsular sinus, medulla, efferent vessel; there are more efferent vessels
options.E: Afferent lymphatics, subcapsular sinus, medulla, cortex, efferent vessel; the capsule is rigid

questions.explanation: Afferent lymphatics bring lymph, which collects in subcapsular sinuses, moves into the cortex then the medulla and exits by the efferent vessel. Fewer efferent vessels let lymph stagnate: a settling tank. A: Cortex precedes medulla after the subcapsular sinus. B: Lymph enters by afferent and leaves by efferent vessels. D: The sinus comes first and efferents are fewer. E: Order and reason are wrong.

questions.stem: Where do naive T and B cells initially sit in a lymph node?

options.A: T cells in the primary lymphoid follicles; B cells in the T-cell areas
options.B: T cells in the medullary cords; B cells in the subcapsular sinus
options.C: T cells and B cells together in germinal centers
options.D: T cells in the T-cell areas; B cells in the primary lymphoid follicles
options.E: T cells in the mantle zone; B cells in the dark zone

questions.explanation: Naive T and B cells entering the node occupy two distinct zones, the T-cell areas and the primary lymphoid follicles (B-cell zones), because of distinct chemokine receptor and chemokine patterns. A: Reversed. B: Not the zones described. C: Germinal centers form after activation. E: These zones belong to an established germinal center.

questions.stem: Which description of follicular dendritic cells is correct?

options.A: Non-hematopoietic, non-phagocytic cells that trap antigen with complement receptors for B cells
options.B: Hematopoietic, phagocytic cells whose long processes present peptide on MHC II to naive T cells
options.C: Non-hematopoietic, phagocytic cells that digest antigen for follicular B cells
options.D: Hematopoietic, non-phagocytic cells that secrete IL-21 for B-cell proliferation
options.E: Non-hematopoietic, non-phagocytic cells that trap antigen through Fc receptors for T cells in the T zone

questions.explanation: FDCs in follicles are of non-hematopoietic origin and non-phagocytic; they bear numerous long processes and trap antigens with complement receptors for access by follicular B cells. B: That describes conventional dendritic cells. C: They are non-phagocytic. D: IL-21 comes from Tfh cells, and FDCs are non-hematopoietic. E: They sit in follicles and use complement receptors for B cells.

questions.stem: After a naive follicular B cell meets its antigen displayed by FDCs or macrophages, where does it go?

options.A: Within a few days to the dark zone of the germinal center
options.B: To the outer follicle, at the interface with the T-cell zone
options.C: Within a few hours to the medullary cords to secrete antibody
options.D: Within a few weeks to the bone marrow as a memory cell
options.E: It stays in the center of the follicle until T cells arrive

questions.explanation: Activated naive follicular B cells migrate within a few hours to the outer follicle, at the interface between the B-cell follicle and the T-cell zone. A: The germinal center forms later. C: Medullary cords receive plasma cells later. D: That is not the first step. E: It migrates to the follicle–T zone interface.

questions.stem: What is linked recognition?

options.A: T cells and B cells activated by different antigens meet in the medulla and interact
options.B: A B cell recognizes two epitopes linked on one receptor
options.C: CD21 and CD19 are linked on the B-cell surface by complement
options.D: Two TCRs are cross-linked by a repetitive polysaccharide
options.E: T and B cells activated by the same antigen meet at the follicle border

questions.explanation: Naive T cells activated by DCs partly become effectors and leave; others migrate to the border with the B-cell follicle, where T and B cells activated by the same antigen meet (linked recognition). A: The same antigen is required. B: Not the definition. C: That describes the coreceptor. D: Cross-linking by polysaccharide concerns BCRs in TI-2 activation.

questions.stem: Put the T–B interaction in order: (1) B cell proliferation and differentiation, (2) helper T cell expresses CD40L and secretes cytokines, (3) B cell presents antigen to the helper T cell, (4) B cell activated by CD40 engagement and cytokines.
questions.explanation: The B cell presents antigen to the helper T cell; the helper T cell is activated, expresses CD40L and secretes cytokines; the B cell is activated by CD40 engagement and cytokines; then it proliferates and differentiates. A: The B cell first presents antigen to the helper T cell. B: CD40L must be expressed before CD40 is engaged. D: Activation precedes proliferation. E: Presentation comes first.

questions.stem: What do activated Tfh cells deliver to B cells through CD40L and through IL-21?

options.A: CD40L–CD40: STAT3 signaling and plasma cell differentiation; IL-21: non-canonical NFκB and anti-apoptotic molecules
options.B: CD40L–CD40: non-canonical NFκB, anti-apoptotic molecules; IL-21: STAT3, proliferation and differentiation
options.C: CD40L–CD40: JAK signaling and class switching to IgM; IL-21: apoptosis of low-affinity cells
options.D: CD40L–CD40: phosphorylation of CD19; IL-21: complement deposition on the pathogen
options.E: CD40L–CD40: release of perforin; IL-21: TLR activation

questions.explanation: CD40L–CD40 activates non-canonical NFκB, inducing anti-apoptotic molecules and B-cell survival. IL-21 binds IL-21R, signals through STAT3 and drives proliferation and differentiation into plasma cells. Other cytokines (IL-6, TGF-β) regulate the type of antibody produced. A: The pathways are swapped. C: Not the effects described. D: CD19 is phosphorylated by the activated BCR. E: Neither is described.

questions.stem: What happens in the primary focus?

options.A: B cells proliferate for several days and some become short-lived plasmablasts
options.B: B cells undergo somatic hypermutation for several weeks, and some become long-lived plasma cells
options.C: B cells rest for several days while T cells proliferate, and class switching is completed
options.D: Resting B cells are displaced to form the mantle zone around light and dark zones
options.E: Memory B cells are selected by follicular dendritic cells and leave by the efferent lymphatic

questions.explanation: In the primary focus B cells proliferate for several days (first phase of the humoral response); some differentiate into antibody-synthesizing plasmablasts. Other B cells go to the follicle and form the germinal center. B: Hypermutation happens in the germinal center. C: B cells proliferate there. D: That describes the germinal center. E: Not what the primary focus is.

questions.stem: How do plasmablasts differ from plasma cells?

options.A: Plasmablasts no longer divide, secrete mainly IgG and migrate to the bone marrow; plasma cells die in the primary focus within days
options.B: Plasmablasts secrete no antibody and wait in the mantle zone; plasma cells secrete IgM in the primary focus
options.C: Plasmablasts are memory cells with membrane antibody; plasma cells are naive B cells
options.D: Plasmablasts still divide and die in the primary focus within days; plasma cells are long-lived cells that migrate to the bone marrow
options.E: Plasmablasts still divide and secrete mainly IgE; plasma cells are short-lived cells of the dark zone

questions.explanation: Plasmablasts have begun to secrete antibody (primarily IgM, intermediate protection) yet still divide and keep B-cell features for interaction with T cells; they die in the primary focus a few days after being generated. Plasma cells are long-lived and migrate to the bone marrow. A: The properties are swapped. B: Plasmablasts have begun to secrete antibody. C: Neither is correct. E: Plasmablasts secrete mainly IgM and plasma cells are long-lived.

questions.stem: Which statement about the germinal center is correct?

options.A: It consists mainly of antigen-specific T cells; proliferating B cells are about 10% of its lymphocytes
options.B: It consists mainly of resting B cells; proliferating B cells form the mantle zone
options.C: It consists mainly of plasma cells; T cells are absent from it
options.D: It consists mainly of follicular dendritic cells; B cells are about 10% of its cells
options.E: It consists mainly of proliferating B cells; antigen-specific T cells are about 10% of its lymphocytes

questions.explanation: Germinal centers are composed mainly of proliferating B cells; antigen-specific T cells represent about 10% of GC lymphocytes and provide help. A: Reversed. B: Resting B cells are pushed out to form the mantle zone. C: Tfh cells are present and provide help. D: B cells predominate.

questions.stem: A follicle that contains a germinal center is called what, and what forms the mantle zone?

options.A: A primary lymphoid follicle; resting B cells displaced to the periphery by proliferating GC B cells
options.B: A secondary lymphoid follicle; Tfh cells surrounding the light and dark zones
options.C: A secondary lymphoid follicle; resting B cells displaced to the periphery
options.D: A primary focus; plasmablasts displaced to the outer follicle
options.E: A secondary lymphoid follicle; follicular dendritic cells of the dark zone

questions.explanation: Follicles with GCs are called secondary lymphoid follicles. Proliferating GC B cells displace resting B cells toward the periphery, forming the mantle zone around the light zone and dark zone. A: A primary follicle has no germinal center. B: The mantle is made of resting B cells. D: The primary focus is a different structure. E: The mantle is made of resting B cells.

questions.stem: When does a germinal center disappear?

options.A: Once plasmablasts form, about 3–4 days after initial exposure
options.B: Once class switching starts, about 3–4 hours after initial exposure
options.C: It persists for life as a secondary follicle
options.D: Once the infection is cleared, about 3–4 weeks after initial exposure
options.E: Once memory cells reach the bone marrow, about 3–4 months after exposure

questions.explanation: The GC shrinks and disappears once infection is cleared (3–4 weeks after initial exposure). A: The germinal center lasts weeks. B: Far too early. C: It shrinks and disappears. E: The time given is 3–4 weeks.

questions.stem: How does complement on a pathogen enhance B-cell activation?

options.A: CD19 binds complement fragments, bringing CD21 near the activated BCR, which cleaves it
options.B: CD81 binds complement fragments and replaces the BCR as the antigen receptor
options.C: CD21 (CR2) binds complement fragments, bringing CD19 near the activated BCR
options.D: CD40 binds complement fragments and substitutes for T-cell help
options.E: CD21 binds the Fc of antibody, cross-linking Fc receptors on the B cell

questions.explanation: The B-cell coreceptor complex contains CD19, CD21 (complement receptor CR2) and CD81. When CD21 binds complement fragments on a pathogen it is brought near the activated BCR; CD19 becomes phosphorylated, enhancing proliferation, differentiation and antibody production. A: CD21 is the complement receptor and CD19 is phosphorylated. B: CD81 is a coreceptor component; CD21 binds complement. D: CD40 binds CD40L. E: CD21 binds complement fragments.

questions.stem: Which statement about somatic hypermutation is correct?

options.A: AID introduces point mutations in the Ig V region; they do not extend to the C region
options.B: AID introduces point mutations in the Ig C region; they do not extend to the V region
options.C: UNG joins V, D and J segments in germinal center B cells
options.D: AID excises DNA between two switch regions to change the V region
options.E: APE1 introduces point mutations across the whole B-cell genome at the same rate

questions.explanation: GC B cells undergo V-region somatic hypermutation (changes of 1–5 amino acids), mediated by AID (activation-induced cytidine deaminase), producing closely related clones; it affects some flanking DNA but does not extend to the C region. B: Reversed. C: V(D)J recombination occurs during development. D: Excision between switch regions is class switching and changes the C region. E: The V region mutates far faster than other DNA.

questions.stem: At what rate do Ig V-region genes accumulate mutations in germinal center B cells, and what does this mean per division?

options.A: About 1/1000 base pairs per division, giving about a 5% chance of a receptor mutation at each division
options.B: About 1/10^10 base pairs per division, giving about a 50% chance of a receptor mutation
options.C: About 1/10 base pairs per division, so each receptor differs after one division
options.D: About 1/100,000 base pairs per division, giving about a 10% chance of a receptor mutation
options.E: About 1/1000 base pairs per division, giving about a 50% chance of a receptor mutation at each division

questions.explanation: Ig V-region genes mutate at about 1/1000 bp per cell division versus 1/10^10 for the rest of the DNA: about a 50% chance of a receptor mutation at each B-cell division. A: The chance given is about 50%. B: 1/10^10 is the rate for the rest of the DNA. C: The rate is 1/1000. D: Not the figures given.

questions.stem: How are mutated germinal center B cells selected?

options.A: Cells with lower affinity are positively selected through contact with FDCs; cells with higher affinity die by apoptosis
options.B: Higher-affinity cells are positively selected via Tfh contact and CD40; cells without a functional BCR die by apoptosis
options.C: Cells with higher affinity are positively selected through TLR signaling; the others become plasmablasts
options.D: Most mutated cells gain affinity and survive; a few die by necrosis
options.E: Cells with higher affinity are negatively selected to prevent autoimmunity; the others become memory cells

questions.explanation: B cells that cannot make a functional BCR or take up antigen well are eliminated by apoptosis (negative selection). B cells with higher affinity (a less frequent event) are positively selected; this involves contact with Tfh cells and CD40 signaling. A: Higher affinity is favored. C: Positive selection involves Tfh contact and CD40. D: Higher affinity is the less frequent event, and death is by apoptosis. E: Higher affinity gives increased survival.

questions.stem: In the cyclic re-entry model, what happens to a centrocyte whose receptor binds antigen better?

options.A: It returns to the light zone, stops dividing and becomes a centroblast
options.B: It leaves by the efferent lymphatic as a plasmablast
options.C: It moves to the mantle zone and becomes a resting B cell
options.D: It undergoes apoptosis to limit clone size
options.E: It returns to the dark zone, divides again and becomes a centroblast

questions.explanation: Centrocytes whose receptors bind antigen better return to the dark zone for additional rounds of division, becoming centroblasts again. Survivors of the GC reaction differentiate into plasma cells or memory cells. A: Re-entry is to the dark zone with further division. B: Plasmablasts arise in the primary focus. C: Not the model described. D: Better binders are favored.

questions.stem: During an immune response, what stays the same and what changes in the progeny of one activated B cell?

options.A: The V region stays the same apart from somatic hypermutation; the C-region isotype may change
options.B: The C region stays the same apart from somatic hypermutation; the V-region specificity may change
options.C: Both V and C regions are replaced by new rearrangements
options.D: Neither changes; different isotypes come from different B-cell clones
options.E: The light chain switches from κ to λ while the heavy chain is fixed

questions.explanation: All progeny of an activated B cell express the same V region (possibly modified by somatic hypermutation) but may express several different C-region isotypes: class (isotype) switching. B: Reversed. C: The assembled V region is kept. D: One clone can switch isotype. E: Class switching concerns the heavy-chain C region.

questions.stem: Which statement about the order of immunoglobulin expression is correct?

options.A: The first receptors are IgM and IgG, the first antibody produced is IgD, and IgA or IgE appear later
options.B: Receptors IgM and IgD first; the first antibody produced is IgM; IgG, IgA or IgE come later
options.C: The first receptor is IgG, the first antibody produced is IgG, and IgM appears in secondary responses
options.D: The first receptors are IgM and IgD, the first antibody produced is IgA, and IgM appears later
options.E: The first receptors are IgD and IgE, the first antibody produced is IgM, and IgG appears later

questions.explanation: The first antigen receptors on B cells are IgM and IgD; the first antibody produced in an immune response is IgM. Later the same V region may be expressed in IgG, IgA or IgE. A: The first receptors are IgM and IgD and the first antibody is IgM. C: IgM comes first. D: The first antibody is IgM. E: Naive B cells carry IgM and IgD.

questions.stem: How does class switching differ from the expression of IgD?

options.A: Class switching is a reversible alternative splicing event directed by cytokines from Tfh cells
options.B: Class switching is an irreversible homologous recombination directed by antigen affinity
options.C: An irreversible non-homologous DNA recombination directed by Tfh cytokines
options.D: Class switching is a point mutation of the V region directed by AID
options.E: Class switching is a rearrangement of V, D and J segments directed by FDCs

questions.explanation: Unlike the expression of IgD, class switching involves an irreversible non-homologous DNA recombination and is directed by cytokines released by Tfh cells. A: It is irreversible DNA recombination. B: It is non-homologous and directed by Tfh cytokines. D: That describes somatic hypermutation. E: V(D)J recombination is a developmental event.

questions.stem: Which statement about switch (S) regions is correct?

options.A: Repetitive DNA sequences downstream of each V-region gene except μ, where RNA polymerase can stall
options.B: Unique DNA sequences upstream of each C-region gene including δ, where AID is transcribed
options.C: Repetitive RNA sequences that guide alternative splicing of μ and δ
options.D: Repetitive DNA sequences upstream of each C-region gene except δ, where RNA polymerase can stall
options.E: Repetitive DNA sequences between V, D and J segments that guide somatic hypermutation

questions.explanation: Switch regions are repetitive DNA sequences that guide class switching, found upstream of each Ig C-region gene with the exception of the δ gene. Transcription through them lets RNA polymerase stall, making them substrates for AID, then UNG and APE1. A: They lie upstream of C genes, and the exception is δ. B: They are repetitive and absent before δ. C: Switch regions are DNA and guide recombination. E: They guide class switching.

questions.stem: In class-switch recombination, in which order do the enzymes act, and what do they produce?

options.A: UNG, then AID, then APE1; single-strand nicks on both strands leading to double-strand breaks
options.B: AID, then UNG, then APE1; single-strand nicks on both strands leading to double-strand breaks
options.C: APE1, then UNG, then AID; point mutations confined to the V region
options.D: AID, then APE1, then UNG; deletion of the V region
options.E: AID, then UNG, then APE1; joining of V, D and J segments

questions.explanation: AID, then UNG (uracil N-glycosylase), then APE1 (apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1) introduce a high density of single-strand nicks into both DNA strands, giving double-strand breaks that are repaired. A: AID acts first. C: Order is wrong and the product is strand breaks in S regions. D: UNG precedes APE1, and the V region is kept. E: The product is breaks in switch regions.

questions.stem: A B cell switches from IgM to IgE. What happens to the DNA?

options.A: The Sμ and Sε regions are transcribed together, and the intervening RNA is spliced out
options.B: The V region is replaced by a new V segment next to Cε
options.C: The Sμ and Sε regions are brought together and ligated, and the intervening DNA is excised
options.D: The Sδ and Sε regions are ligated after excision of Cμ
options.E: The Cμ gene is mutated by AID until it encodes ε

questions.explanation: The two S regions are brought together by repair proteins; class switching is completed by excision of the intervening DNA and ligation of the Sε and Sμ regions (switching from IgM to IgE). A: Switching is DNA recombination with excision. B: The V region is unchanged. D: There is no switch region before δ. E: Switching removes intervening DNA; it does not mutate Cμ into Cε.

questions.stem: How many subclasses do IgG and IgA have in humans, and how are IgG subclasses named?

options.A: IgG has four subclasses, IgG1 to IgG4, named in increasing order of serum abundance; IgA has two
options.B: IgG has two subclasses and IgA has four, named by order of discovery
options.C: IgG has three subclasses named by molecular weight; IgA has two
options.D: IgG has four subclasses named by half-life; IgA has one
options.E: IgG has four subclasses, IgG1 to IgG4, named in decreasing order of serum abundance; IgA has two

questions.explanation: IgG has 4 subclasses in humans (IgG1, IgG2, IgG3, IgG4, named by decreasing abundance in serum); IgA has 2 (IgA1, IgA2). A: The order is decreasing abundance. B: Reversed numbers and wrong naming rule. C: IgG has four. D: Naming is by abundance, and IgA has two.

questions.stem: Which statement about IgM is correct?

options.A: Secreted as a pentamer with 10 antigen-binding sites, it has high avidity and activates complement
options.B: Secreted as a dimer with 4 antigen-binding sites, it has high avidity and crosses the placenta
options.C: Secreted as a pentamer with 10 antigen-binding sites, it is the principal antibody of extracellular fluid
options.D: Secreted as a monomer with 2 antigen-binding sites, it makes up 80% of plasma immunoglobulin
options.E: Secreted as a pentamer after class switching, it requires T-cell help to be made

questions.explanation: IgM is the first class produced, under 10% of plasma Ig, secreted as a pentamer (high molecular weight, stays in the bloodstream) with 10 antigen-binding sites: high avidity for multivalent antigens and effective complement activation. Some IgM is produced without T-cell help. B: A dimer with 4 sites is IgA, and IgM does not cross the placenta. C: Its size keeps it in the bloodstream; IgG is the principal antibody. D: That describes IgG. E: IgM is produced first, and some is made without T-cell help.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is expressed on all naive B cells together with IgM, yet little of it is produced as antibody at any time?

options.A: IgG
options.B: IgA
options.C: IgE
options.D: IgD
options.E: IgG4

questions.explanation: All naive B cells express surface IgM and IgD. Little IgD antibody is produced at any time. A: IgG is the principal antibody of blood. B: IgA is the principal antibody of secretions. C: IgE is present at very low levels but is not the naive B-cell coreceptor isotype. E: A subclass of IgG.

questions.stem: A newborn has protective antibody against tetanus although he has never been immunized. Which class of maternal antibody explains this, and which further properties does the lecture give it?

options.A: IgM: it can cross the placenta, has a plasma life of about 3 weeks and activates complement
options.B: IgG: it can cross the placenta, has a plasma life of about 3 weeks and opsonizes efficiently
options.C: IgA: it can cross the placenta, has a plasma life of a few days and neutralizes toxins
options.D: IgG: it can cross the placenta, has a plasma life of a few days and is a weak complement activator
options.E: IgE: it can cross the placenta and binds mast cells of the fetus

questions.explanation: IgG is the principal antibody in blood and extracellular fluid, has a long life in plasma (about 3 weeks versus a few days for the others), efficiently opsonizes, activates complement, and is able to cross the placenta (the slide attributes this to its size; standard texts attribute it to a specific Fc receptor). A: IgM does not cross the placenta. C: IgA is the antibody of secretions and does not cross the placenta. D: Its plasma life is about 3 weeks and it activates complement. E: IgE does not cross the placenta.

questions.stem: Which statement about IgA is correct?

options.A: It is the principal antibody of secretions including breast milk and acts mainly by neutralization
options.B: It is the principal antibody of secretions including breast milk and acts mainly by opsonization
options.C: It is the principal antibody of blood and acts mainly by complement activation
options.D: It is found as a pentamer in secretions and binds mast cells avidly
options.E: It is secreted by plasma cells of the bone marrow and crosses the placenta

questions.explanation: IgA is the principal class in secretions including breast milk, mostly secreted by the epithelial lining of the GI and respiratory tracts; it functions mainly as a neutralizing antibody (not a potent opsonin, weak complement activator) and exists as monomers or dimers. B: It is not a potent opsonin. C: IgG is the principal blood antibody, and IgA is a weak complement activator. D: IgA is a monomer or dimer; mast-cell binding is IgE. E: It is mostly secreted at GI and respiratory epithelia.

questions.stem: Which statement about IgE is correct?

options.A: Present at high levels in secretions, it is bound avidly to receptors on mast cells and neutralizes toxins
options.B: Present at very low levels, it is bound avidly to receptors on neutrophils and activates complement
options.C: Present at very low levels, it forms pentamers that agglutinate parasites in blood
options.D: Present at very low levels, it is bound avidly to mast-cell receptors and drives allergic reactions
options.E: Present at about 13% of serum antibody, it is the main opsonin against helminths

questions.explanation: IgE is present at very low levels in blood or extracellular fluids, is bound avidly to receptors on mast cells, and plays a crucial role in allergic reactions. A: IgE levels are very low. B: The receptors named are on mast cells (and basophils). C: Pentamers are IgM. E: 13% is the figure for IgA.

questions.stem: According to the Ig isotype table, which values are correct?

options.A: IgG: about 6% of serum antibody, MW 900,000; IgM: about 80%, MW 150,000
options.B: IgG: about 80% of serum antibody, MW 900,000; IgM: about 13%, MW 150,000
options.C: IgG: about 50% of serum antibody, MW 150,000; IgM: about 30%, MW 385,000
options.D: IgG: about 80% of serum antibody, MW 200,000; IgM: less than 1%, MW 900,000
options.E: IgG: about 80% of serum antibody, MW 150,000; IgM: about 6%, MW 900,000

questions.explanation: Table: IgG 150,000, 80%, 2 sites, crosses placenta, fixes complement; IgM 900,000, 6%, 10 sites; IgA 385,000 as dimer, 13%, 4 sites; IgD and IgE under 1%. A: Reversed. B: Molecular weights are swapped and 13% is IgA. C: Not the table values; 385,000 is dimeric IgA. D: IgG is 150,000 and IgM about 6%.

questions.stem: After affinity maturation and class switching, where do the resulting plasma cells go?

options.A: Some to the thymus, where a subset is long-lived; others to the cortex of lymph nodes or the white pulp of the spleen
options.B: They stay in the light zone of the germinal center for life
options.C: Some to the bone marrow (long-lived subset); others to lymph node medullary cords or splenic red pulp
options.D: Some to the bone marrow as plasmablasts; others to the mantle zone as resting B cells
options.E: They circulate in blood as IgM-secreting cells and die within days

questions.explanation: Some B cells exit from the light zone and differentiate into plasma cells; some migrate to the bone marrow where a subset live for a long period, others to the medullary cords of lymph nodes or the red pulp of the spleen. B cells activated in mucosal GCs and switched to IgA remain in mucosal tissues. A: The sites are bone marrow, medullary cords and red pulp. B: They exit from the light zone. D: Not the fates described. E: That resembles plasmablasts.

questions.stem: A patient with a helminth infection has parasites coated with antibody. NK cells bind the antibody and release damaging substances. Which mechanism is this, and what does it allow?

options.A: ADCC: NK cells recognize the Fab of antibody, so adaptive effectors can attack pathogens that display PAMPs
options.B: Opsonization: phagocytes recognize C3b, so the parasite is engulfed
options.C: Neutralization: antibody blocks parasite toxins without effector cells
options.D: ADCC: NK cells recognize the Fc of antibody, so innate effectors can attack pathogens that lack or hide PAMPs
options.E: Complement activation: the MAC lyses the parasite after C1q binds Fc

questions.explanation: Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity: NK cells recognize the constant fragment (Fc) of antibodies and release damaging substances. ADCC lets innate effectors recognize pathogens that do not express PAMPs or hide them; it is a big part of the response to parasites. A: Recognition is of the Fc, and the benefit concerns pathogens lacking or hiding PAMPs. B: The scenario describes NK cells and antibody Fc. C: NK cells are involved here. E: The effector here is the NK cell.

questions.stem: Antibodies contribute to immunity in three ways. What are they, and what influences which one is used?

options.A: Neutralization, opsonization and complement activation; the light-chain type of the antibody
options.B: Neutralization, opsonization and complement activation; the heavy-chain isotype of the antibody
options.C: Neutralization, phagocytosis and antigen presentation; the heavy-chain isotype of the antibody
options.D: Agglutination, class switching and affinity maturation; the V region of the antibody
options.E: Neutralization, opsonization and complement activation; the affinity of the antigen-binding site

questions.explanation: Antibodies act by neutralization, opsonization and complement activation; the choice of effector mechanism is influenced by the heavy-chain isotype (class). A: The class (heavy-chain isotype) is what matters. C: The three ways are neutralization, opsonization and complement activation. D: The last two are B-cell processes. E: The choice of mechanism is influenced by isotype.

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as influencing the type and quantity of antibody produced EXCEPT:

options.A: The type of antigen
options.B: Prior antigen exposure
options.C: Involvement of T cells
options.D: The anatomic site where activation occurs
options.E: The MHC class I haplotype of the plasma cell

questions.explanation: Type and quantity of antibodies vary with the type of antigen, prior antigen exposure, involvement of T cells and the anatomic site where activation occurs. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed.

questions.stem: What does the clonal selection hypothesis explain, according to the take-home messages?

options.A: Random mutations during clonal expansion yield higher-affinity B cells, making secondary responses effective
options.B: Random mutations during clonal expansion yield B cells with new specificities, which is why primary responses are so fast
options.C: Directed mutations by antigen yield B cells with lower affinity, which limits autoimmunity
options.D: Class switching during clonal expansion yields IgM memory, which is why secondary responses are slower
options.E: Negative selection in the thymus removes B cells, which is why tolerance is maintained

questions.explanation: During clonal selection, random mutations during clonal expansion produce B cells with increased antibody-binding affinity; this may explain why secondary immune responses are so effective at preventing reinfection. B: The gain is affinity, and the benefit is for secondary responses. C: Mutations are random and higher affinity is selected. D: Not the hypothesis. E: Not what is described.

questions.stem: Besides CD40L and IL-21, activated Tfh cells secrete cytokines such as IL-6 and TGF-β. What do these signals regulate?

options.A: The affinity of each binding site for its epitope
options.B: The survival of B cells through non-canonical NFκB
options.C: The type of antibody produced
options.D: The migration of B cells to the T-zone interface
options.E: The cross-linking of B-cell receptors by antigen

questions.explanation: Tfh cells secrete additional cytokines (IL-6, TGF-β and others) that provide signals regulating the type of antibodies produced. A: Affinity is changed by somatic hypermutation and selection. B: That is the CD40L–CD40 effect. D: Migration is chemokine-driven. E: That depends on the antigen.
